title: Currency of the Thirteen Colonies
summary: Before the dollar, money depended on where you stood.
introduction: There was no single colonial currency. A pound changed value from colony to colony, foreign coins circulated everywhere, and each paper issue carried its own legal and financial terms.

interpretation.title: How to read a colonial note
introduction: A colonial note combined several independent terms: its face denomination, accounting unit, valuation, redemption mechanism, monetary status, method of issue and intended lifespan. None of those terms alone explains what the paper was worth or why it circulated.
Use these sections as a shared vocabulary. The colony stories then show how those terms changed over time and where each collected note sits in that history.

concepts.title: The amount printed on the note
paragraphs: The denomination is the face amount: ten shillings, four pounds, four dollars. It tells a user how many named units the note represents.
It does not, by itself, identify the unit's value in another colony, promise immediate payment in coin, or make the note legal tender. Those are separate terms.

facts.label: Face amount
facts.text: The number and unit named on the paper

facts.label: Separate questions
facts.text: What that unit was worth, how it could be redeemed and what the law required

concepts.title: The unit of account organized prices and debts
paragraphs: A unit of account is the language used to record value. Pounds, shillings and pence supplied a familiar arithmetic—twelve pence to a shilling and twenty shillings to a pound—even where few British coins circulated.
Each colony's £sd unit could differ from sterling and from neighboring colonial money. Dollar accounting increasingly appeared during the Revolution, but older units continued beside it.

facts.label: Not an equivalence
facts.text: £1 colonial money did not necessarily equal £1 sterling

concepts.callout: The accounting unit measured the debt; it was not necessarily the object used to pay it.

concepts.title: Valuation connected local units to accepted references
paragraphs: Colonies rated familiar coins—especially the Spanish dollar—in local shillings and pence. The same coin could therefore be valued at different numbers from one colony to another, and those ratings could change over time.

A note might state a silver weight, a sterling rate or a standard such as Proclamation Money. Such language defines how to value the denomination; it does not automatically promise immediate exchange at a treasury.
concepts.callout: A valuation rule translates units. A redemption promise says what the issuer must eventually pay.

concepts.title: Redemption explains how the obligation returned
paragraphs: Redemption was the mechanism intended to bring a note back to its issuer or discharge the debt. Tax-funded bills returned when holders paid public dues; Loan Office bills returned through borrowers' scheduled repayments.
Other issues promised payment at a future date in specie, sterling bills or another defined asset. The date, funding source and form of payment mattered as much as the amount printed on the face.

facts.label: Tax redemption
facts.text: Bills return through future taxes or public dues

facts.label: Loan redemption
facts.text: Bills return through principal and interest payments

facts.label: Specified payment
facts.text: The issuer pays a named asset on or after a stated date

concepts.title: Monetary status defined what the paper could legally do
paragraphs: Legal tender status could require a creditor to accept a note for qualifying debts. A note might instead be receivable only for taxes or public debts, circulate by agreement without compulsory status, or function as an interest-bearing Treasury obligation.

These categories were not interchangeable. The Currency Acts restricted colonial legal-tender powers, but did not make every paper issue impossible; public receivability and future redemption could still support circulation.

facts.label: Legal tender
facts.text: The law requires acceptance for specified debts

facts.label: Tax receivable
facts.text: The issuer accepts the paper for public dues

facts.label: Circulating credit
facts.text: People accept the paper because they trust its terms and future use

concepts.title: Issuance identifies the authority, purpose and route into circulation
paragraphs: An issue began with an authorizing government, act, date, total amount and purpose. A legislature might spend bills on war or public works before collecting later taxes; a Loan Office might lend them against land or other security.

Signatures, serial numbers, printers and anti-counterfeiting devices authenticated individual notes. A change from colony to state, or from pounds to dollars, can make a political transition visible on the paper itself.

concepts.title: Most notes were designed to leave circulation
paragraphs: An issue could expire, return through taxes or loan repayments, be exchanged for a later issue, or become invalid after a deadline. Depreciation and emergency laws often changed that planned path.
Redeemed notes were commonly punched, slashed, cut or otherwise cancelled. Those marks may document the successful end of the obligation rather than ordinary damage.

interpretation.relatedIntroduction: The colonies were not monetary islands. Spanish silver, sterling bills and Portuguese gold crossed borders, while French North America developed its own experiments with paper and credit.

story.subtitle: From wartime bills to successive standards
paragraphs: New Hampshire first issued bills of credit in 1709 to meet wartime expenses. Those notes were meant to return through future taxes, but repeated emissions left the colony reckoning in a depreciated Old Tenor currency.

Reform came in stages rather than all at once: New Tenor appeared in 1742, Lawful Money in 1755 and another colonial standard in 1763. Each new scale had to coexist with older notes and older habits of accounting.

The missing snapshot should come from the 1742 New Tenor issue. Such a note would catch the colony at the moment it tried to reset value without yet escaping the accumulated history of Old Tenor paper.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1742 New Tenor note that makes New Hampshire's first major revaluation visible.

story.subtitle: From the first public bills to silver—and back
paragraphs: Massachusetts Bay issued £7,000 in 1690 after a failed expedition against Canada, creating the first government paper currency in English North America. What began as an emergency expedient became a recurring way to meet public costs.

By mid-century, depreciation and the competing paper of neighboring colonies had made that system untenable. British reimbursement for Louisbourg helped Massachusetts redeem its bills in silver in 1749–1750, and the colony largely withdrew from paper circulation.

The missing snapshot should be a 1775 Massachusetts note, when war reopened the question and revolutionary authority again issued public paper. It would show bills returning after a generation in which silver—not provincial notes—had been the official answer.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1775 Massachusetts note documenting the revolutionary return to government paper.

story.subtitle: From wartime bills to New Tenor and state paper
paragraphs: Rhode Island entered paper money in 1710 to finance the Annapolis Royal expedition. Its first bills were legal tender, receivable for taxes and scheduled to be retired, but the colony did not stop after that emergency passed.

Repeated issues—many placed through public loan banks—expanded the supply and weakened Old Tenor. Rhode Island introduced New Tenor in 1740 and Lawful Money in 1763, then returned to heavy wartime issuance under revolutionary government.

The missing snapshot should be a 1740 New Tenor note. It would show the colony acknowledging depreciation in the denomination itself and trying to establish a new scale while Old Tenor remained part of everyday reckoning.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1740 New Tenor note marking Rhode Island's explicit reset of its paper-money scale.

story.subtitle: From colonial bills to interest-bearing state debt
paragraphs: Connecticut first issued bills of credit in 1709 for wartime needs. Like its New England neighbors, it later moved from Old Tenor to New Tenor and then to Lawful Money as depreciation changed what a shilling meant.

Independence changed the issuing authority and the financial form, but not every monetary habit. During the Revolution, the State used Treasury Notes that could circulate while also bearing interest toward a stated maturity.

The collected ten-shilling note dated July 1, 1780 is a snapshot of that hybrid moment. It still counts in £sd, yet it names the State, earns 5 percent interest and promises payment in Spanish milled dollars by March 1, 1785.

reading.title: Why this moment matters
paragraphs: Political authority changed faster than monetary language. The note preserves the old ten-shilling account while recasting circulating paper as an explicitly dated, interest-bearing obligation of the State.

story.lookClosely: A slash or punched hole can indicate successful redemption, transforming an active claim into evidence that the claim had already been discharged.

story.subtitle: From tax-backed provincial bills to state dollars
paragraphs: New York began issuing bills of credit in 1709 to meet military expenses, with future taxes intended to bring the paper back. The notes counted in local £sd even though Spanish silver supplied an important practical reference.

That local scale remained distinctive: a Spanish dollar commonly counted as eight New York shillings. During the Revolution, new political authorities increasingly named dollar values directly instead of expressing every obligation through provincial pounds.

The missing snapshot should be a 1776 State of New York dollar note. It would place the collection at the point where the issuer and the denomination both began to describe a post-colonial monetary order.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1776 State of New York note denominated in dollars.

story.subtitle: From early bills to secured, closely guarded paper
paragraphs: New Jersey began issuing bills of credit in 1709 for military expense, then used later emissions and public lending to make government paper a durable part of provincial finance. Over time, the problem shifted from introducing paper to keeping its value and identity credible.

The 1763 issue reflects that mature system. It defined each denomination by a silver-weight equivalent, gave the authorized bills long legal life and introduced mica-flaked paper as a defense against persistent counterfeiting.

The collected twelve-shilling counterfeit is a snapshot of that system from its vulnerable edge. Its maker copied the official monetary language and appearance closely enough to test whether New Jersey's safeguards and public trust could be imitated.

facts.label: Form
facts.text: Contemporary counterfeit of a Bill of Credit

reading.title: Why this moment matters
paragraphs: New Jersey's paper had become established enough that credibility depended on both written terms and recognizable manufacture. The counterfeit records exactly which features an imitator believed the public would trust.

story.lookClosely: The 1763 issue introduced mica-flaked paper to New Jersey currency. This counterfeit invites comparison between the security material and the imitation of official design.

story.subtitle: From Loan Office paper to wartime state finance
paragraphs: Pennsylvania's 1723 paper entered chiefly through a public Loan Office. Borrowers pledged land, spent the notes into circulation and repaid principal and interest over time, allowing credit expansion and retirement to follow a planned cycle.

War changed that model. Provincial military issues placed paper through government spending, and independence transferred the authority to a Commonwealth facing immediate army costs and much greater pressure to issue quickly.

The collected £4 note dated April 10, 1777 is a snapshot of that wartime turn. It retains Pennsylvania's pound account, but its named issuer is now the Commonwealth and its £200,000 issue was authorized specifically for army support.

reading.title: Why this moment matters
paragraphs: The object shows institutional change without a clean monetary break: a new Commonwealth finances a revolutionary army through the inherited language of Pennsylvania pounds.

story.lookClosely: Pound denominations carried a farming scene on the reverse. John Dunlap—printer of the first broadside Declaration of Independence—printed the issue on watermarked paper.

story.subtitle: From mortgage lending to Revolutionary finance
paragraphs: The Lower Counties' 1723 Loan Office put £5,000 into circulation through loans secured by first mortgages on real estate. Borrowers spent the notes and returned them through scheduled principal and interest payments.

Later provincial issues mixed that credit system with tax-supported public finance. Independence then shifted the issuer from the Lower Counties to the State of Delaware and made wartime expenditure—not mortgage lending—the immediate reason to create paper.
The missing snapshot should be a 1777 State of Delaware note. It would show the old regional £sd account surviving while the authority and purpose printed above it had become revolutionary.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1777 State of Delaware note documenting the shift from provincial credit to wartime state finance.

story.subtitle: From funded provincial paper to dollar notes
paragraphs: Maryland's 1733 currency law created a provincial paper system supported by a sinking fund managed in London. The structure tied local circulation to assets and future settlement rather than relying only on a promise to accept the notes for taxes.

After Parliament restricted new legal-tender bills, Maryland's issues of 1767–1775 adopted a different compromise: dollar denominations, no compulsory private acceptance and a specified future payment in sterling.

The collected four-dollar note dated April 10, 1774 is a snapshot of that compromise. It circulated without legal-tender status because the province promised eventual payment at 4s6d sterling per dollar through the funded system.

facts.label: Printers
facts.text: Anne Catherine Green and Frederick Green

reading.title: Why this moment matters
paragraphs: Maryland preserved a circulating paper medium after imperial restrictions by separating public credibility from legal-tender compulsion. This note makes the alternative—precise future settlement—visible.

story.lookClosely: The thin paper contains mica flakes and nature-print security designs. The note came from the Annapolis shop of Anne Catherine Green and her son Frederick.

story.subtitle: From resistance to wartime Treasury Notes
paragraphs: Virginia relied on tobacco, coin and book credit longer than most colonies and resisted a government paper currency. The French and Indian War finally broke that policy in 1755, when the colony authorized Treasury Notes to meet military expenses before taxes could be collected.

What began as a wartime exception became a repeatable fiscal tool. Virginia issued further tax-backed notes through 1774, then revolutionary government changed the authority on the paper and increasingly used dollar denominations.
The missing snapshot should be a note from the first 1755 emission. It would capture the precise moment when scarcity and war pushed Virginia from resisting paper money to relying on it.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1755 Virginia Treasury Note from the colony's first paper-money emission.

story.subtitle: From emergency bills to a named valuation standard
paragraphs: North Carolina began issuing bills of credit in 1712 amid war, debt and a shortage of usable coin. Repeated emissions kept public finance moving, but depreciation forced the colony to distinguish older paper from later accounting scales.

New Tenor appeared in 1748. The 1754 issue went further by identifying Proclamation Money as its valuation standard, an effort to make the meaning of the local shilling more explicit before revolutionary government later moved toward dollars.

The collected forty-shilling note dated March 9, 1754 is a snapshot of that stabilizing effort. It remains a provincial legal-tender bill in £sd, but the note itself tells the holder which monetary standard governs those forty shillings.

reading.title: Why this moment matters
paragraphs: The note sits between depreciated early bills and revolutionary dollar paper. Its unusually explicit standard shows the province trying to repair the meaning of a familiar unit rather than abandon it.

story.lookClosely: The forty-shilling note carries Christ Church at Newbern. Other denominations use a butterfly, boar, swan, bear, squirrel, crown, Bible and other motifs.

story.subtitle: From public-bank credit to a transformed pound
paragraphs: South Carolina issued bills of credit in 1703 and soon made paper a regular instrument of public finance. A public loan bank added another route into circulation, lending government notes on security instead of spending every issue directly.

Repeated emissions and depreciation transformed the local pound. By the revolutionary era, a Spanish dollar could be reckoned at roughly 32s6d in Charleston—a striking departure from both sterling and the shilling scales used farther north.

The missing snapshot should be a 1778 State of South Carolina note. Its state authority and inherited £sd denomination would place the political revolution beside the colony's already transformed accounting system.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1778 State of South Carolina £sd note linking new political authority to the colony's distinctive valuation scale.

story.subtitle: From London claims to provincial and state paper
paragraphs: Trustee Georgia first used Sola Bills: transferable claims that circulated locally but ultimately returned to London for payment. Their value depended on a transatlantic promise rather than on a mature local treasury system.

Royal government changed that arrangement in 1755 by creating a General Loan issue, placing locally issued paper through secured loans and using part of the proceeds for public works. Revolutionary state notes later redirected paper toward wartime finance under a third authority.
The missing snapshot should come from the 1755 General Loan. It would mark Georgia's move from circulating London claims to a provincial paper system created and managed within the colony.
story.collectingGoal: Collecting target: a 1755 Georgia General Loan note documenting the colony's shift to locally issued public credit.

artifacts.title: 1754 40s North Carolina Forty Shillings
artifacts.description: Forty shillings means £2 in North Carolina's local accounting system—not £2 sterling. The phrase Proclamation Money relates that local denomination to a standard expressed against specie, making the difference between a unit of account and its value standard visible on one note.
artifacts.subtitle: A local pound defined by Proclamation Money
researchNotes: The March 9, 1754 issue authorized £40,000 in legal-tender bills of credit at Proclamation Money rates.
The forty-shilling denomination shows Christ Church at Newbern and was printed from an engraved copper plate.

artifacts.title: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit
artifacts.description: New Jersey's authorized issue translated local paper denominations into stated silver-weight equivalents. This specimen is a contemporary counterfeit: evidence that recognition, security materials and public trust were as much a part of the monetary system as the legislature's promises.

images.alt: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 1
1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 2

artifacts.subtitle: A silver-referenced currency, convincingly imitated
researchNotes: Recorded as Fr. NJ-156CT and identified in the collection as a contemporary counterfeit of the twelve-shilling denomination.
The December 31, 1763 authorized issue was legal tender through 1781, became invalid after 1782 and introduced mica-flaked paper to New Jersey currency.

artifacts.title: 1774 $4 Maryland Colonial Currency
artifacts.description: This note was not legal tender. Maryland instead promised future payment at 4s6d sterling per dollar, so its $4 denomination equaled 18 shillings sterling. The dollar names the paper; sterling states its settlement value.
artifacts.subtitle: Four dollars measured by a future sterling promise
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. MD-68, serial number 14042.
Anne Catherine Green and Frederick Green printed the issue on thin paper containing mica flakes and nature-print security designs.

artifacts.title: 1777 Pennsylvania £4 Note
artifacts.description: Pennsylvania authorized £200,000 of this issue for army support. The Commonwealth used paper to command resources before equivalent revenue arrived; later exchange and invalidation laws completed the note's path from wartime issue to retirement.
artifacts.subtitle: Paper issued to finance an army
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as PA-224a, serial number 10507, with Eric P. Newman Collection provenance.
John Dunlap printed the issue. Pound denominations carried a farming scene on the reverse and the paper was watermarked PENSYL / VANIA.

artifacts.title: 1780 Connecticut 10-Shilling Treasury Note
artifacts.description: This ten-shilling Treasury Note promised payment in Spanish milled dollars by March 1, 1785 and carried 5 percent annual interest. Its denomination, maturity and interest clauses make it closer to a government security than to an indefinitely circulating modern banknote.
artifacts.subtitle: Circulating paper and an interest-bearing state debt
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. CT-238, serial number 3063.
Redeemed examples were commonly cancelled by slashing or punching holes through them.

artifacts.title: Banque Royale January 1, 1720. 10 Livres
artifacts.description: The Banque Royale promised to pay the bearer on sight in silver specie. Its bank liability differs from a colonial legislature's bill of credit and places British-American experiments within a wider Atlantic monetary world.
artifacts.subtitle: A bank's on-sight promise to the bearer
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as P-A16b and records a PMG grade of Very Fine 30.
The Banque Royale was tied to the Compagnie des Indes and French Louisiana finance, but the exhibit does not claim these notes themselves circulated in America.
